headline: A 2014 Senate bill that was not adopted would have given businesses a tax credit for moving operations back to the U.S. and removed deductions for moving them overseas.
what_it_does: If adopted, the bill would have let businesses claim a tax credit worth up to 20% of expenses for closing a business located outside the United States and relocating it within the United States. It would also have barred businesses from deducting costs of moving a U.S. business operation overseas. To claim the credit, a business would have needed to increase its number of full-time U.S. employees.

who_it_affects.group: Businesses that move operations from outside the U.S. back to the U.S.
who_it_affects.how: They would have been able to claim a tax credit of up to 20% of qualifying relocation expenses, if they increased full-time U.S. employment.

who_it_affects.group: Businesses that move U.S. operations to other countries
who_it_affects.how: They would have lost the ability to deduct expenses tied to relocating a U.S. business outside the country.

who_it_affects.group: Full-time workers in the United States
who_it_affects.how: The bill tied the insourcing tax credit to growth in full-time U.S. jobs at the claiming business.
